Claude Code hooks: a practical guide from the video

What Claude Code hooks do, how to wire one, and the two mistakes the video demonstrates.

By Daniel Agrici · 2026-09-03 · 1 min read · 303 words

Hooks let Claude Code run your own commands before or after a tool call. In the video Claude Code Hooks Explained, Daniel Agrici builds one hook from scratch and shows two mistakes that silently disable it. This guide follows the same path in reading order, with a link to the exact moment for each step.

Key Takeaways - A hook is a shell command bound to a tool event; the settings file decides when it runs. - Test a hook with a no-op command first (02:14). - Two common mistakes: a missing executable bit and a matcher that never matches.

What is a Claude Code hook?

A hook is a shell command that Claude Code runs when a named event fires, such as a tool call about to start. The video defines it at 00:42: the command receives the tool input as JSON on stdin and can allow, block, or annotate the call with its exit code.

Wiring the first hook

Watch this moment: 01:30. The hook lives under .claude/hooks/ and the settings file names it under a PreToolUse matcher.

Step Command Moment
1 chmod +x .claude/hooks/format.sh 02:40
2 Add the matcher to settings.json 02:12 
chmod +x .claude/hooks/format.sh

Common mistakes

Exit status 126 means the hook file is not executable (03:55)

The second mistake is a matcher that never matches. The video shows the fix at 04:20: match the tool name exactly, not the file pattern.

Frequently asked questions

Does a hook run on every tool call?

No. A hook runs only for the events and matchers named in the settings file, so a PreToolUse hook with a Bash matcher ignores file edits.
